webpage.text:
Asbestos saga proves our feeble press watchdog has no bark and no bite | Science

Back in February, the Daily Mail published an article denouncing "The Great Asbestos Hysteria", and claiming that the health risks had been grossly exaggerated by "the BBC, profiteering lawyers, and gullible politicians".

The article was a response to a study raising concerns about the ongoing dangers of asbestos in UK schools. Those dangers were, the Daily Mail assured us, "all but non-existent". While many older school buildings still contained asbestos, almost all of it was "relatively harmless white asbestos, encapsulated in cement or other materials, from which it is virtually impossible to extract even a single dangerous fibre". The threat from such products was so "vanishingly small" that a study by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) had concluded that the danger was "insignificant", with "arguably zero" risk of lung cancer.

Good news all round, then. No need for schools to worry about that crumbling asbestos roof. No need, we might think, for maintenance workers to wear protective clothing when renovating old school buildings. No need, it would seem, to employ specialist contractors to assess whether to leave asbestos undisturbed or get it removed. Those guys are, in any case, according to the Mail, a "commercial racket" with a "vested interest in exaggerating the dangers of products which are, in effect, harmless".

Last week, seven months after the article was published, the Daily Mail issued a carefully worded correction:

> "...The HSE assessments related to specific levels of exposure to white asbestos fibres, not white asbestos products, and found a risk from higher levels. The article said that asbestos in UK schools is almost all white. According to the HSE the more harmful brown asbestos was also frequently used in schools..."

Not such good news. What many reading the Daily Mail article won't have known is that the author, Christopher Booker, has a long track record of downplaying the health risks of white asbestos. Though not a scientist himself, Booker has written at least 42 newspaper articles on this subject since 2002, making claims that run counter to the views of most experts, but are remarkably similar to those of the asbestos industry.

Several of the claims in the Daily Mail article – including that an HSE study once concluded the health risks of white asbestos cement were "insignificant" - have previously appeared in Booker's Sunday Telegraph column, prompting a series of direct rebuttals from the HSE. The available evidence, as assessed by – among others - the World Health Organisation, the UK and US governments, and the European Union, is that white asbestos poses a serious risk to human health that needs to be carefully managed.
If the experts are right about asbestos and Booker is wrong, then this matters for at least two reasons. Firstly, there's a danger that people may take unnecessary risks when handling the stuff, with potentially deadly consequences a couple of decades down the line. In 2008, a survey by the British Lung Foundation found widespread ignorance about the health risks, with under a third of tradespeople – the group most at risk of exposure – aware that it could cause cancer, and 28% "mistakenly assuming that some levels of asbestos are safe". Further misinformation surely won't help.
Secondly, for those affected by asbestos-related disease, ill-informed media reports belittling the health risks can be offensive and upsetting. I got the smallest glimpse of what that must be like when I saw that my blog had been linked to from a Facebook group set up by mesothelioma sufferers in response to Booker's Daily Mail article.

Several members of the group had decided to report the Mail to the Press Complaints Commission, for breaching section 1 of the PCC's ethical code: "The Press must take care not to publish inaccurate, misleading or distorted information". I've been following Booker's antics for a while – I researched his work in detail for my book Don't Get Fooled Again, and still write about him from time to time on my blog. So I decided to support the Facebook campaigners – and test out the PCC's claim to be "fast, free and fair" – by putting in a complaint of my own.

It wasn't difficult to produce evidence debunking the Mail's assertion that white asbestos was "relatively harmless". Back in 2002, the HSE had published a summary, with references, of the peer-reviewed research linking the material to mesothelioma and lung cancer. The newspaper's claim that an HSE study had found the dangers of white asbestos cement to be "insignificant" was also easy to disprove: Booker had made the self-same claim in the Sunday Telegraph back in 2008, and been rebutted in detail by the HSE.

Neither was it hard to show that the Mail had got it wrong in claiming that "it is virtually impossible to extract even a single dangerous fibre" from white asbestos cement. An HSE lab report from 2007 notes that "the claim that respirable airborne chrysotile fibres are not able to be released from asbestos cement products was refuted by the individual airborne fibres sampled during the breaking of the test sample with a hammer".

In theory, this should have been the end of the matter. According to the PCC's code, "a significant inaccuracy, misleading statement or distortion once recognised must be corrected, promptly and with due prominence". What happened instead, in my view, speaks volumes both about the character of the Daily Mail, and the credibility of the newspaper industry's self-regulatory body.

After a delay of several weeks, the PCC forwarded me a dismissive response from the Daily Mail's executive managing editor, Robin Esser. While acknowledging some minor errors, Esser insisted that the disputed HSE study did indeed back up Booker's views on asbestos. The fact that the HSE had put out a statement explicitly rebutting this merely proved that "those responsible for HSE press releases are similarly unable to grasp the significance of findings published by their own statisticians". For good measure, Esser accused me (falsely, just in case you're wondering) of being "allied to a well-organised and well-funded commercial lobby", who "stand to benefit financially" from the "anti-asbestos campaign".

Rather than take ownership of the process, assess the various bits of evidence and come to a judgement, the PCC instead asked me to go through this new set of claims and produce a further response. Here I began to see why so many people have given up on the PCC. If a newspaper digs in its heels and simply denies all the evidence that's been presented, there doesn't seem to be much that the PCC can do except bat the issue back to the complainant.

It was at this stage that I learned that the asbestos campaigner Michael Lees had also submitted a detailed complaint. Michael, who has been working to highlight the dangers of asbestos in schools since losing his wife Gina, a teacher, to mesothelioma, had been singled out by name – the third time that Booker had done this. Michael took particular exception to the dismissive terms in which the article had referred to his wife's death, adding to the offence of a previous piece in which Booker had dubbed the case "bizarre". He was also concerned that – aside from Booker's views on white asbestos – the article sidestepped the fact that many schools still contain large amounts of brown asbestos, whose dangers are beyond dispute.

More time-consuming exchanges followed, with long gaps in between, while we awaited a response from the Daily Mail. In the end we won, sort of. The newspaper agreed to make some amendments to the text of the article, publish a short correction, and write a private apology to Michael Lees over Booker's comments about his wife. But to get even this far has taken seven months, and a substantial time investment, while the Daily Mail seems to have been able to drag the process out with impunity. "Free", perhaps – but hardly "fast", or "fair".

Richard Wilson is the author of Don't Get Fooled Again – The Skeptic's Guide to Life. www.twitter.com/dontgetfooled

Bucks County District Attorney's Office's Post


----------------------------------------


Bucks County District Attorney's Office

April 6  ·
In this week's Legal 101, we’re tackling one of the most misunderstood terms in the courtroom: Hearsay.
In its simplest form, hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered in court to prove that the matter asserted is true. Essentially, it’s a witness testifying about something they didn't see or hear themselves, but were told by someone else.
The law prefers firsthand knowledge. But there are exceptions, such as excited utterances, public records, previous court testimony and dying declarations.
#legal101

How institutional secrecy hampers court reporting on public health issues

Introduction by Croakey: Open government and legal systems are critical to media reporting on a range of public health issues, including fossil fuels, tobacco, family violence and gambling, as well as in matters affecting First Nations rights and wellbeing.

A recent report claims the concept of open justice, where court proceeding should be open to public and professional scrutiny, is under threat in Victoria from increased police, public service and government secrecy.

Croakey’s Associate Professor Fiona Martin reports below on its findings and implications for elsewhere in Australia.

----------------------------------------


Fiona Martin writes:

Effective reporting of legal actions with public health implications, like specialist malpractice, hospital mismanagement, tobacco control or domestic violence, is essential to public and professional awareness of these issues and campaigns for policy reform.

Investigations into Robodebt, for example, revealed the targeting of vulnerable people who relied on income support and the mental health toll of the Federal Government’s dodgy algorithmic welfare debt recovery scheme.

Public interest journalism of course plays a critical role in this, which is why Croakey is concerned about a new report on the crisis in public interest reporting of Victorian courts.

It reveals major implications for communication of contentious case, public health practice, and access to health system information.

The State of Play: limitations to public interest journalism in Victoria research report, commissioned by the Melbourne Press Club and conducted by Monash University, argues that there is a systemic breakdown in judicial transparency and government accountability, which is keeping the public in the dark about important legal actions.

In the study, senior journalists say they are now encountering some of the worst constraints on court reporting of their careers, due to increased restrictions on access to basic legal information, government and police sources, and difficulties with freedom of information requests.

Based on interviews with 12 of Victoria’s most experienced reporters from major news outlets, the research shows that the historical concept of open justice, where court proceeding should be open to public and professional scrutiny, is under threat from increased police, public service and government secrecy.

The report also highlights how suppression orders are increasingly being used to conceal the identity of high-profile defendants, including alleged rapists, on mental health grounds — with Victorian courts issuing more orders than other states across Australia.*

Croakey spoke with report co-author Monash University’s Associate Professor Johan Lidberg to find out where and why institutional secrecy was causing problems for reporting of public health isssues, and what could be done about it.


Reasons for secrecy

Lidberg told Croakey that growing information centralisation and control in the Victorian Labor Premier’s office was also part of the background to increased state departmental secrecy, with a lack of challenge by a weakened Liberal Opposition contributing.

However, he said the lack of transparency about public interest information provision cuts across “the whole system” – courts, governments and police.

“Police in Victoria are quite unwilling to even speak off the record anymore. Maybe that’s partly because they’re sunburnt by the whole Lawyer X thing, and, you know, they’re scared for repercussions.”

A lack of funding for the public servants meant to deal with FOI requests was also preventing them getting to journalists’ requests, with “government after government starving FOI teams of resources.”

As well, Lidberg noted the number of working journalists has fallen dramatically in the last decade, with well over 5,000 jobs lost since 2011 and increasing casualisation of the workforce. PR and communications roles now far outnumber those in news media, and he says “media advisors know that journalists lack the time and resources to pursue information.”


Secrecy across the spectrum

Asked if the situation was comparable across other states and territories, Lidberg said there were certainly similar issues in New South Wales, and a trend nation-wide to “greater secrecy across the government spectrum.”

It is certainly the case in Tasmania, where a 2025 independent review of Tasmania’s Right to Information (RTI) framework by Professor Tim McCormack and Adjunct Associate Professor Rick Snell from the University of Tasmania found a systemic culture of “non-disclosure and obfuscation”.

Their study was based on consultation with 75 individuals and organisations, including all government departments, local councils, major political parties, community members and frequent users of the RTI system.

Federal transparency is also weak with the Centre for Public Integrity showing increasing government secrecy over the terms of the last two Prime Ministers, based on departmental failures to respond to Senate orders to produce documents and FOI requests.

However, the Albanese Government has just failed in its bid to further tighten FOI law, withdrawing the  the Freedom of Information Amendment Bill 2025 when it was set to be rejected in the Senate.

In a dissenting Parliamentary Committee report into the Bill, independent Senator David Pocock argued it should be rejected because it “expands Cabinet secrecy, weakens the pro-disclosure objects clause, neuters the public-interest test, bans anonymous freedom of information (FOI) requests used by whistleblowers and journalists, and imposes new financial barriers.”


Freedom of information?

This should be good news for the public health sector. Freedom of Information (FOI) requests have been central to reporting of Australian health scandals, including  ABC News’ revelation that pathology companies were rorting Medicare for COVID-19 tests during the pandemic.

But journalists interviewed for the State of Play report indicated investigative work like this was difficult because they were hampered by excessive delays on meeting FOI requests, given unreasonable justifications for rejections and deliberately exhausted into giving up by repeated changes in the process.

Lidberg, who was involved in federally funded research into FOI implementation across Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia, said it found health and hospitals was a “particularly fraught area”, because of the legal complexity.

He said FOI officers and coordinators in certain jurisdictions had to consider different and overlapping acts that could affect FOI requests, including mental health, child safety and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health as well as laws around mandatory notification. That “made it very hard for them to determine what to release and not to release,” he said.

FOI staffing shortages and training were critical problems, as was uneven digitisation of records, with people having to search multiple systems and even data on floppy disks. Another factor slowing up processing of media requests in Victoria was where individuals had been advised to seek their personal records through FOI, and hospitals were “being swamped” by those applications.

Officers were also worried when releasing documents about breaching privacy and the confidentiality of clients, staff and those who work or volunteer for them.


Suppression orders

While, as Guardian Australia has reported, suppression orders can be critical, for example, for the safety of whistleblowers, child witnesses and victims of sexual assault, the State of Play report also highlighted concerns that they are routinely used to cloak the identity of defendants. It concludes that Victoria’s Open Courts Act 2013, which was designed to reduce such orders and improve open justice, has “largely failed”, as they have increased since its introduction.

One journalist noted that he’d seen a problematic trend in “high-profile people charged with serious offences who are able to argue for suppression orders using the evidence of people who say that it will be detrimental to their mental health if they are identified.”

Certainly women’s rights activists have been concerned these orders can be used to protect powerful men from prosecution in family violence cases.

Recently, Federal Court Chief Justice Debbie Mortimer discussed why she had rejected an attempt by the Northern Territory Government to suppress the settlement sum in a class action involving children held at the notorious Don Dale detention centre.

She observed that “[i]t is difficult to conceive of a piece of litigation which is more centrally concerned with the administration of justice than this one.”

Lidberg acknowledged that suppression orders are essential for protection of vulnerable witnesses such as women fleeing domestic violence or testifying against organised crime, but argued there can be good grounds for challenging them.

At the Melbourne Press Club launch of State of Play, former Supreme Court justice Betty King, KC, suggested that some psychiatrists were abusing the open courts system by producing reports on clients that were then used to seek mental health-based suppression orders.

According to The Age, she said psychiatrists posed the greatest threat to courts’ transparency, as they wrote untested psychiatric reports which led to suppression orders, and argued that these reports “should be tested in court.”

Victoria’s Chief Justice Richard Niall and a number of key legal bodies have reportedly rejected the report’s findings, arguing they misrepresent the facts and overlook the essential role suppression orders play in safeguarding the integrity of the justice system.

However, a campaign by major news media outlets has prompted Victorian Attorney-General Sonya Kilkenny to seek advice on possible changes to suppression order laws on mental health grounds.


What else can be done?

Since the release of the report, media organisations and the courts have been talking about ways to restore open communication of legal information, including regular meetings between the editors, journalists, court media teams and the Chief Justices, a past practice that had somehow fallen by the wayside during the pandemic.

Lidberg said the Open Courts Act also needs review, but that that could take years. In the meantime, he said it was important that stakeholders in public interest journalism engage with judicial system and talk to its leaders, the Chief Justices, about ways to improve open justice.

The report recommends they should also, where possible, support journalists to accurately and safely report on the administration of justice.

Centrally State of Play recommends that the FOI system be reformed.

In that respect the defeat of the Federal Government’s FOI amendments has been welcomed by civil society groups. The Centre for Public Integrity is calling for reform, with Open Australia arguing that governments need to better resource FOI teams, enforce compliance with requests, and foster a culture of disclosure.

----------------------------------------

*Updated 17/03/26: This article was amended from saying Victorian courts are responsible for almost half (47 percent) of the orders issued across Australia, as the numbers are contested. See MediaWatch 16/03/26.  Associate Professor Johan Lidberg says based on the raw numbers of suppression orders reported to newsrooms across the country Victoria appears to have issued the highest number, but the figures are contestable as the suppression order reporting regimes vary across jurisdictions.

----------------------------------------

Top 5 Traits Of Successful Digital Content Leaders

Glen Hale


Glen Hale

Published Feb 26, 2017

I consider myself extremely fortunate in my role leading digital content and audience development for Gray Television to work with many highly skilled, highly effective digital content leaders both on the corporate and local level. Over the course of my now 19 years in digital content leadership, I have identified the types of behaviors that correspond to the strongest leaders, along with those that frequently predict failure. There’s really no need to focus on the negative, especially since we’re all here to learn how to improve as leaders, employees and people. To that end, I put together this quick list of what I believe to be the top 5 traits of successful digital content leaders. There are, of course, many more positive traits that predict long term success. Maybe there’s something I missed that should be on this list.

Efficiency -- The ability to not only juggle but excel at tackling multiple tasks simultaneously is highly desirable. Prioritization capabilities are of utmost importance. The most efficient digital content leaders quickly identify mission-critical needs and avoid wasting time and resources on things that ultimately don’t matter that much. That discernment is the distinction between good and great digital content leadership.

Resourcefulness -- Digital content leaders who have a knack for identifying and leveraging the right people and tools are almost always effective. This involves identification of needs and evaluation of the proper mechanisms and expertise needed to harness them. Great digital leaders then turn their findings into products and services that blaze trails, serving needs that in many cases people didn’t know they had before but then find essential.

Creativity -- The best digital content leaders often find themselves strategizing about ways to optimize or otherwise improve upon existing products, dreaming up new content offerings and using the tools already available to them in new ways to improve audience engagement and retention. Great digital content leaders aren’t disheartened when a new initiative fails. They view it as a learning experience that can be built upon to create a successful project the next time.

Articulation -- Effective communication is of paramount importance toward building high-performing teams, recruiting others to believe in a vision and selling that vision both up and down the leadership chain. This includes the constant refinement of written and verbal communication skills. Digital content leaders who are adept at both are able to inspire employees, peers and their bosses to their best work with unwavering, consistent effort.

Adaptability -- I chose to save what I believe to be the most important trait for last. There is no more desirable trait in digital content leaders than adaptability. Nearly all industries today are fast-moving, but the goalposts for digital employees move constantly. Leaders have to grapple with emerging methods to reach audiences, ever-changing audience demands and technological/platform advancements. Leaders who recognize when the targets move and thrive in that environment will almost always be highly successful.

What did I miss?
